headlines.title: Stellantis CEO urges incentives for carmakers who build in Europe as Chinese rivals gain ground
headlines.summary: Stellantis' CEO urged European regulators to create incentives for carmakers to manufacture vehicles in the region amid competition from Chinese rivals.
headlines.article_text: Stellantis CEO urges rewards for Europe carmakers amid Chinese competition Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Stellantis CEO told CNBC that Europe needs to incentivize carmakers who build in the region. It comes as Chinese carmakers are quickly accelerating their share of the European car market. Shares of Stellantis, known for its key car brands such as Jeep and Ram, rose in early trade Monday after the EU and China reached an agreement to cut the number of hybrid cars China exports to the bloc. In this article RNO-FR FAU-FF STLA Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 3:12 03:12 Stellantis CEO backs level playing field for all carmakers Squawk Box Europe Stellantis' CEO has called on European regulators to create stronger incentives for carmakers to manufacture vehicles in the region, as it faces intensifying competition from Chinese rivals that are dominating the market. Antonio Filosa, who has served at the helm of the automotive giant since 2025, spoke with "CNBC Conversation" ahead of the Paris Motor Show on Monday about the company's declining sales amid China's "impressive" acceleration in the European market. "What we are supporting a lot in Europe is to establish for everybody a level playing field," Filosa said in an interview with CNBC's Charlotte Reed . "In concrete terms, it means to work on true regulation... starting from "Made in Europe," that should be regulation that incentivizes, rewards, and protects the ones that are able to demonstrate that they design cars, engineer cars," Filosa added. Made in Europe refers to proposed legislation drawn up by the EU Commission which would require carmakers to meet minimum local content requirements to sell within the regional market. The global carmaker, which is known for its key car brands such as Jeep and Ram, has been in the midst of a $70 billion turnaround strategy as it struggles with declining demand. The company's shares are down almost 60% so far since the beginning of the year. Stellantis' shares since the beginning of the year. Chinese car brands are dominating the global market , with their global auto-sales share jumping by nearly 70% from 2020 to 2025, according to market research and consulting firm GlobalData. Meanwhile, the market share of European car sales was close to zero in 2020, but is up to 12% in August this year, according to data from Germany-based Dataforce. "I believe that Chinese automakers, the ones that we know, can really offer many consumers in many segments, good technology, and competitive prices," Filosa said. European trade commissioner Maroš Sefčovič said Friday that China has agreed to halve its exports of hybrid cars to the bloc, after Beijing had repeatedly rejected requests. European carmakers moved higher Monday morning after news of the agreement. Stellantis added 2.7% and French carmaker Renault were up around 3%. French automotive parts suppliers Valeo and Forvia also rose in early trading. A spokesperson for China's Ministry of Commerce responded on Monday to the request, saying that China and the European Union have maintained a dialogue on trade and investment and reached "several consensuses and achievements that are conducive to maintaining a stable and balanced key trade partnership," according to CNBC's translation from Chinese to English. As part of the agreement, one principle laid out was "non-discrimination," which says that no measures will specifically target or discriminate against Chinese companies. "China's quota will not be lower than that of any other import source for the EU." — CNBC's Michael Wayland helped contribute to this report. AI may change the price of your Big Mac and groceries — what this means for shoppers
headlines.summary: As retailers turn to AI tools to streamline operations, experts warn that collecting more detailed consumer data increases the risk of personalized pricing.
headlines.article_text: How AI and dynamic pricing may change the price of your groceries Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Supermarkets and fast food giants are increasingly using artificial intelligence to digitize their operations. Some have been accused of using so-called "dynamic pricing" to set rapid real-time changes in prices that could dramatically affect shoppers' experiences. Experts told CNBC that this could raise the risk of shoppers facing more individualized prices. In this article MCD TSCO-GB KR WMT AMZN Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT People pick up their menu inside the McDonald's restaurant in Times Square, Manhattan, on Sept. 29, 2026, in New York City. KHemaz | GVN | Getty Images Fast-food giants and supermarkets are rolling out a range of AI tools that could affect the prices shoppers pay, but experts warn the spread of data-driven tools could make personalized pricing easier to deploy. Just this week, a federal antitrust lawsuit filed against McDonald's alleged the fast food giant uses an AI-powered "pricing engine" to set menu prices across U.S. locations and overcharge customers for Big Macs and fries. McDonald's has denied that it's using AI to determine what individual customers are willing to pay and said it provides its franchisees with "tools, resources, research and recommendations to help them make informed decisions." Even so, food businesses globally are increasingly digitizing operations with AI. Earlier this year, American grocery chain Kroger said it's using an AI platform called FlashFood to mark down perishables nearing the end of their shelf life and marketing them to shoppers via an app. Meanwhile, electronic shelf labels (ESLs), which display prices on digital screens, are becoming increasingly popular at supermarkets like Kroger, Walmart , and Amazon Fresh. Whole Foods Market spokesperson Rachel Malish said the supermarket chain "does not use dynamic pricing" in a statement to CNBC. Malish said that digital shelf labels "simplify the price tag change process for our employees [and] reduce paper waste from traditional tags." watch now VIDEO 6:05 06:05 How Walmart's digital shelf labels could change shopping CNBC Digital Original Video The technology is also gaining traction among U.K. supermarkets such as Tesco , Morrisons, and Asda. Morrisons declined to comment to CNBC on its ESLs . The British Retail Consortium's director of food & sustainability, Andrew Opie, has said that supermarkets have "no intention to use dynamic or surge pricing in their stores," and that digital pricing is instead a way of updating and checking prices quickly. More recently, global financial platform Revolut trialed facial recognition checkout in select coffee shops, allowing customers to pay with just a picture at checkout. The technology relies on a pre-existing selfie ID that Revolut customers submit as part of standard security checks for comparison, but no additional information is collected. CNBC reached out to Tesco and Asda for comment on the use of AI tools but did not receive a response. As AI use becomes normalized among retailers, experts warn that this could lead to more dynamic pricing, which refers to frequent, rapid real-time changes in prices that could dramatically affect shoppers' experiences. "Dynamic pricing means changing prices in response to changing market conditions, such as demand, timing, capacity or competitors' prices," Miroslava Marinova, a senior lecturer of commercial law at the University of East London, told CNBC. "It is not new. Airlines, hotels, and ride-hailing services have used it for years." Bank of England economists Clare Lombardelli and Rupal Patel said in April that more sophisticated technology is leading to prices changing more frequently and also becoming more individualized, which could see more firms charging "as close to the maximum price a consumer is willing to pay for a good or service," which they defined as "perfect price discrimination." These conditions could make it harder for statisticians to "measure and interpret" month-to-month inflation data, as the consumer price index is based on a representative sample of prices for shoppers. "That works well when prices mostly move slowly and uniformly. But when prices shift continually – and differently for each shopper – the idea of a 'representative' price becomes strained," the BOE economists added. AI collects more consumer data While dynamic pricing has been in play for a long time, the BOE economists and Marinova noted that AI tools such as ESLs and facial recognition checkout are changing the amount of information that companies can collect on consumers, from transaction histories to browsing behavior, location, and purchasing patterns. On Wednesday, U.K. supermarket chain Sainsbury's released "SmartLists," an AI feature that helps customers create shopping lists and find products just by uploading pictures of what they need or by typing out meal ideas. CNBC reached out to Sainsbury's for comment but did not hear back immediately. "This is also why the traditional distinction between dynamic and personalised pricing is becoming less clear in practice," Marinova explained. "Dynamic pricing responds primarily to market conditions, whereas personalised pricing uses information about the consumer to estimate willingness to pay." As companies use both pricing systems, it raises questions around whether customer information is being used to determine the prices consumers see. "As retailers combine market-level information with increasingly detailed consumer data, the boundary between dynamic and personalised pricing becomes thinner," Marinova added. Walmart and Kroger have publicly insisted in recent years that they do not use dynamic or surge pricing to set individualized prices for customers, but have instead used tools to streamline operations. Several U.S. states are moving to curb data-driven pricing. New York requires most businesses using customers’ personal data to set prices to disclose it clearly. Maryland has restricted food retailers and delivery services from using personalised, data-driven pricing to charge higher prices for certain food, while New Jersey and Connecticut have enacted measures targeting “surveillance pricing.” Consumer choice compromised Dynamic and personalized pricing are not automatically bad for shoppers, Marinova said, explaining that it can discount items for some consumers, making some products and services more accessible. However, the risk of individualized pricing is that consumers are no longer aware of whether the price they're getting reflects general market conditions or if it's been influenced by information about their own behavior. "That makes it much harder to compare prices and to know whether another consumer is being offered a different price for the same product," she said. "If consumers cannot understand why they received a particular price, cannot compare it with prices offered to others, and cannot effectively switch to another supplier, the normal disciplining effect of consumer choice becomes weaker." The BOE economists added that an additional challenge is that personalized pricing "splinters the consumer experience," which means households will face increasingly different inflation rates. "And when prices differ for the same thing, inflation becomes even more personalised – and aggregate measures may no longer reflect households' experience," they said.
